newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Cuba policy sparked self-mutilation wave.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Cuba policy sparked self-mutilation wave.

text.p: A 1994 U.S. decision to detain Cubans seeking to reach the United States at the Guantanamo Bay naval base unless they had a serious medical problem sparked a wave of self-mutilation and faked injuries, according to report in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.

The injuries and illnesses usually occurred in waves and were fuelled by the U.S. decision to allow people flown to the United States for medical treatment to remain in the country, according to Dr. Thomas C. Andrews and his colleagues at the Wilford Hall Medical Centre at Lackland Air Force Base in Texas.

For example, when one person with serious burns was airlifted to the United States for special care, several other Cubans subsequently appeared at the detention center's medical facilities with serious burns.

Two migrants inserted diesel fuel into their leg or scrotum, another forced a length of electrical cord into his body, while others ingested rocks, pins and batteries hoping that the doctors at the base would be unable to treat them and they would be airlifted to the United States.
Five men severed their Achilles' tendons. Others tried to fake comas (they were "revived" with smelling salts). Many claimed to have heart problems.

"Pseudoseizures were so common that whenever the hospital commander walked through the camps on informal tours of inspection, several people fell to the ground with convulsions," the doctors reported.
"These cases illustrate graphically how Cuban migrants attempted to use self-mutilation and malingering to gain entry into the United States," the Andrews team said.
The cases stopped when it was announced that the detainees could enter the United States.

Andrews and his colleagues said that if future cases arise, the United States should either provide comprehensive medical care at the detention centre or adopt a different policy where detainees who are sent to the mainland for treatment are returned once their medical care is finished.
The United States needs to recognise "that providing humanitarian relief -- in this case, adequate medical care -- may lead to feigned illness in some circumstances," they said.

Almost all of the Cubans detained at Guantanamo eventually were flown to Florida as part of a May 1995 migration accord between Washington and Havana that also allowed the United States to return to Cuba migrants picked up at sea.
